label: Four-Dimensional Geometry
notes: This chapter, printed pages 396 through 412, opens four-dimensional Euclidean space for inspection. We treat a point as a length-four vector and accept that no screen shows everything at once. The guiding question is which claim survives projection, slicing, or sampling once a coordinate is hidden.

label: Coordinates in R4
notes: A point in four dimensions is an ordered quadruple of real numbers, and distance generalizes Pythagoras across all four axes. The fourth axis is genuinely perpendicular to the familiar three; it is not time and not a trick, simply one more independent direction we cannot embed in our visual field.

label: The Analogy Ladder
notes: Each dimension is built by sweeping the previous figure along a fresh perpendicular direction. A point sweeps to a segment, a segment to a square, a square to a cube, and a cube to a tesseract. Vertex counts double at every rung, giving sixteen vertices for the four-dimensional measure polytope.

label: Building the Tesseract
notes: The measure polytope, or hypercube, is the unit cube swept one unit along the fourth axis. Sweeping doubles the old vertices and joins each to its copy, producing sixteen vertices and thirty-two edges. Its boundary is built from eight cubic cells, twenty-four square faces, and these thirty-two edges.

label: Counting the 8-Cell
notes: The hypercube carries a full face ledger: sixteen vertices, thirty-two edges, twenty-four square faces, and eight cubic cells. Each count follows from the binomial pattern of choosing which coordinates stay fixed at zero or one and which range freely across the unit interval in four-dimensional space.

label: The Tesseract Shadow
notes: Projecting from a point beyond the fourth axis yields the cube-within-a-cube Schlegel diagram. The near cubic cell appears large, the far cell small, and eight slanted edges connect corresponding vertices. The picture deliberately distorts length and angle while preserving incidence, which is exactly the structure we want to read.

label: Slicing the 16-Cell
notes: The sixteen-cell is the four-dimensional cross-polytope, the unit ball of the l-one norm. Fixing the fourth coordinate at level t leaves a three-dimensional octahedron of radius one minus the absolute value of t. As the plane advances toward a vertex the octahedron shrinks, its volume falling by a cubic law.

label: Six Regular Polytopes
notes: Four dimensions admit exactly six regular convex polytopes: the five-cell simplex, the tesseract, the sixteen-cell, the twenty-four-cell, the hundred-twenty-cell, and the six-hundred-cell. This count exceeds the five Platonic solids of three dimensions, yet collapses to only three regular polytopes in every dimension five and above.

label: The Euler-Poincare Check
notes: The boundary of a four-polytope is a closed three-dimensional complex, so its alternating face count vanishes: vertices minus edges plus faces minus cells equals zero. This identity audits every f-vector in the table; a miscounted edge or cell almost always shows up as a broken Euler sum, catching errors cheaply.

label: Why Four Is Special
notes: Dimension two hosts infinitely many regular polygons, dimension three exactly five Platonic solids, dimension four a surprising six polychora, and every higher dimension only three. The twenty-four-cell, self-dual and with no three-dimensional analogue, is the exceptional figure responsible for four dimensions being uniquely rich.

label: D4 Close Packing
notes: The densest equal-sphere packing in four dimensions is the D4 lattice. Its root shell consists of the twenty-four vectors with two nonzero entries of plus or minus one, all of norm root two. Hence each sphere touches twenty-four neighbors, and the lattice achieves packing density pi squared over sixteen.

label: Synthesis
notes: Every four-dimensional representation should declare what it forgets. Projection discards metric scale but keeps edge incidence; slicing hides one coordinate but leaves a concrete octahedron. Schlafli symbols, the Euler relation, and packing invariants give complementary checks on what a flat shadow of a four-dimensional figure may honestly claim.
